source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's HOU3-HOU4 campus in Houston publishes 84 MW of IT capacity across 347,000 square feet, the largest published figure of any facility mapped in Texas.

The density implied by those two numbers is about 242 square feet per megawatt. That is a floorplan fact, not a compute fact. It says nothing about what silicon goes inside, and the operator publishes no rack density. At 40 kW per rack, 84 MW is roughly 2,100 racks. At 10 kW per rack, it is roughly 8,400. The gap between those two numbers decides whether this campus matters to AI, and the spec page cannot resolve it. The one certification listed, Green Globes, is a whole-building environmental rating, which speaks to general commercial occupancy rather than to any specific tenant or workload. No tenant, accelerator count, power procurement, or interconnection status is published.

Texas is the deepest market mapped, with 137 facilities, but only 19 publish a megawatt figure at all. Those 19 total 475.41 MW, so this single campus is 17.7 percent of all published Texas capacity. That share is a statement about disclosure as much as about construction. Most of the state's mapped footprint is invisible in capacity terms, so one operator willing to publish a number can top a ranking without that ranking meaning what it appears to mean.

What the data does not cover is the part that would settle the AI question: no tenant, no chip count, no power contract, no grid interconnection. The 84 MW is a nameplate for the building, and the building is the constraint the site tracks, but the load it will actually carry is not in these facts.
